meta.title: Who really said "Sin has many tools, but a lie is the handle which fits them all"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Edmund Burke. The line opens Chapter VI of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, first printed in April 1858.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Sin has many tools, but a lie is the handle which fits them all'?
meta.ogDescription: Burke never wrote it. Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. did - it is the opening sentence of Chapter VI, The Atlantic Monthly, April 1858.

answer.label: Not Edmund Burke — actually Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
answer.sourceLine: The line is not Burke’s. It is the opening sentence of Chapter VI of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table by the American physician and essayist Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., first printed in The Atlantic Monthly for April 1858 and collected in book form the same year. Burke died in 1797, and the sentence appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Burke page — not in its sourced list, and not in its attributed, disputed or misattributed lists either.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Atlantic Monthly, Vol. I, No. VI — April 1858

source.excerpt:
Sin has many tools, but a lie is the handle which fits them all.

——I think, Sir,—said the divinity-student,—you must intend that for one of the sayings of the Seven Wise Men of Boston you were speaking of the other day.
trail: The sentence opens Chapter VI of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table — it is the chapter’s very first line, before any dialogue begins: Wikisource, Chapter 6 ↗. An independent transcription of the same chapter reads identically, down to “which fits them all”: Eldritch Press ↗.
It reached print first in the magazine serial. The instalment in The Atlantic Monthly, Vol. I, No. VI ↗ opens with the same sentence, and that issue is headed “VOL. I.—APRIL, 1858.—NO. VI.” ↗

The book edition transcribed on Wikisource carries the imprint “PHILLIPS, SAMPSON AND COMPANY. M DCCC LVIII” ↗, and describes the book as a collection of essays published in The Atlantic Monthly between 1857 and 1858.

On the attribution side: Wikiquote lists it among Holmes Sr.’s sourced quotations ↗, under The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table (1858), Chapter 6, while Wikiquote’s Edmund Burke page ↗ does not carry the line in any section. No Quote Investigator article on this quote could be found.
source.excerptNote: The aphorism is the chapter’s first line, dropped without preamble, and the table answers it at once. The Autocrat brushes off the divinity-student’s jab, saying he would have to say something better than that before claiming a place among the Seven Wise Men, and then goes on to defend the point at length.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was published in April 1858, in The Atlantic Monthly, Vol. I, No. VI, and collected the same year in the Phillips, Sampson and Company book edition of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table. Both are long before the 1931 cut-off, so the text is in the public domain in the United States. It was written in English, so no translation rights are involved.

author.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
author.heading: Who was Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.?
author.metaLine: 1809–1894 · American physician, poet and Harvard anatomy professor
author.bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was a Boston physician and writer who held the Parkman Professorship of Anatomy and Physiology at Harvard Medical School from 1847 to 1882, serving as dean until 1853. He was also one of the founding voices of The Atlantic Monthly — he supplied the magazine’s name and wrote for it for decades, most famously the Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table columns, monthly instalments of invented boarding-house table talk. He was the father of the Supreme Court justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., a resemblance of names that has quietly rerouted a great many of the father’s sentences to the son.

misattribution.heading: Three ways this quote goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This is a sentence with a documented author, a documented book and a documented month of publication — and it still circulates under two other names and in two different wordings. Here is what to watch for.

items.why: Quote databases print it flatly as Burke’s, with no source of any kind — QuoteDB ↗ is a typical example, and the credit has spread from pages like it across social media. Burke died in 1797; the sentence was printed in 1858. It is also absent from Wikiquote’s Burke page ↗ in every section, including the ones for disputed and misattributed lines.

items.who: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., the Supreme Court justice
items.why: The Quotations Page ↗ files it under “Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.,” described there as a “US jurist (1841 - 1935),” and names its source only as a collection called Poor Man’s College. The justice was the essayist’s son. Wikiquote flags the pattern outright: “Many quotes attributed to Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. were actually authored by his father, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr.” ↗

Holmes wrote which fits them all — that is the reading in the April 1858 magazine text and in the book chapter. Poster and quote-card versions routinely substitute “that,” often stacking the two errors together: Quotefancy ↗ sells it as “that fits them all,” under Holmes Jr.’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: Holmes Sr. opened Chapter VI with it, word for word, in the April 1858 Atlantic Monthly — read the chapter ↗. Every other name on the card was attached later.

context.heading: Why it reads like a proverb
lead: Holmes wrote the Autocrat as monthly table talk for the brand-new Atlantic Monthly — a magazine he had named himself — and he liked to open an instalment with a hard little aphorism and then let the boarders take swings at it. This is one of those openings: the April 1858 number begins with the sentence and nothing else, no scene-setting, no speaker introduced.

The reply comes immediately. The divinity-student needles the Autocrat for sounding like one of the “Seven Wise Men of Boston” he had been mocking earlier, and the Autocrat waves the compliment away, saying he would have to do better than that to qualify. The line was built to sound quotable, which is precisely why it detached from its book and went wandering.
detailsBody: The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table ran as a serial in The Atlantic Monthly across 1857 and 1858 before Phillips, Sampson and Company of Boston collected it as a book in 1858. Chapter VI of the book is the instalment printed in Volume I, Number VI, dated April 1858, and that instalment opens with this sentence.
Holmes had used the Autocrat title twice before, in The New-England Magazine in November 1831 and February 1832, and reworked the idea when the Atlantic launched.
context.pull: It opens the chapter cold — one sentence, no preamble — and the next voice at the table is already arguing with it.
